title: Adaptive ingress connection warmup for bursty tenants
author: Priya Raman
content:
Overview

This guide describes the recommended adaptive connection warmup pattern for customers that exhibit highly bursty traffic at onboarding or after a policy change. The goal is to reduce 502/503 spikes, prevent ingress-proxy CPU spikes, and ensure steady, observable ramping of backend capacity for Dedicated and Private tenants. This is intended for Customer Success (CS), Solutions Engineering, and Eng-Infra/SRE teams who coordinate on new tenant cutovers, scale tests, or major product rollouts.

When to use this guide

- New enterprise customers expected to go from test traffic to production burst (e.g., sudden nightly batch, scheduled marketing sends, or unpredictable chatbots).
- Customers migrating to Dedicated instances where tenant-specific warmup helps autoscaler behavior.
- Known bursty workloads that previously caused connection churn, increased 5xxs, or token-processing backlog.

Goals and SLO alignment

- Keep ingress-level 5xx rate <= 0.2% during ramp windows.
- Ensure 95th percentile request latency at ingress proxy < 350 ms for short sequences during warmup (customer baseline may differ).
- Avoid cold-start-style resource contention that causes model-serving GPU preemption or long queueing.

Owner and stakeholders

- Primary owner: Customer Success (CS) - Onboarding & Escalations (owner: Priya Raman).
- Engineering partners: Eng-Infra (networking/ingress), Eng-Serving-Runtime (kernel/batching), Eng-SRE (autoscaling, capacity).
- Customer contacts: Solutions Engineer and Customer Platform/DevOps representative.

High-level approach

1) Classification: identify the tenant’s traffic profile (burst amplitude, events/s, average tokens per request).
2) Adaptive warmup policy: implement progressive connection and request rate increases using client-side and edge-side pacing.
3) Observability & gating: evaluate health via real-time dashboards and synthetic probes during each step.
4) Containment & rollback: automated throttles and failback paths if error thresholds exceed safe limits.

Pre-cutover checklist (CS + SE)

- Confirm tenant capacity profile: expected peak RPS, average token length, concurrency budget.
- Assign SRE on-call for the cutover window and notify Eng-Infra 24h ahead.
- Create a temporary warmup policy in the tenant config namespace (see examples below).
- Schedule synthetic traffic harness run and baseline snapshot 2 hours before cutover.

Example policy (edge-side):

This YAML snippet demonstrates an ingress-side warmup policy applied via the edge-sidecar config. Replace placeholder values with tenant-specific parameters.

---
apiVersion: redwood.io/v1
kind: WarmupPolicy
metadata:
  tenant: tenant-acme-inc
spec:
  initial_connection_limit: 20              # initial half-open connections allowed
  connection_ramp: [20, 50, 150, 500]      # connections by step
  step_duration_sec: 600                   # 10 minutes per step
  request_rate_cps: [5, 20, 80, 300]       # requests per second per connection pool
  health_gate:
    max_5xx_rate_pct: 0.2
    max_ingress_cpu_pct: 70
    max_queue_latency_ms: 500
  backoff_policy:
    on_threshold_breach: scale_down_step
    cooldown_sec: 300
---

Client-side recommendations

- Encourage the customer to use exponential backoff with jitter for retries (max 3 attempts) and a capped concurrency.
- Provide a lightweight reference client that respects server-supplied warmup tokens and per-connection rate hints. Example HTTP header: X-Redwood-Warmup-Window: step=2;allowed-cps=20.

Step-by-step warmup playbook

1) Step 0 — Preparation (T-120 to T-10 minutes)
   - Validate tenant config and warmup policy presence.
   - Start synthetic probe job hitting representative endpoints at low CPS (2–5 cps).
   - Take baseline telemetry snapshot (ingress 50/95/99 latencies, 5xx rates, edge CPU).

2) Step 1 — Initial connections (T=0 to +10 minutes)
   - Allow initial_connection_limit connections and enforce request_rate_cps[0].
   - Observe for anomalous 5xx increase or client retransmissions.
   - If health_gate breached: trigger backoff (see Containment).

3) Step 2 — Moderate ramp (+10 to +20 minutes)
   - Increase connection limit to connection_ramp[1] and CPS to request_rate_cps[1].
   - Validate KV cache hit ratios and runtime queue depths (should be trending down).

4) Step 3 — High ramp (+20 to +30 minutes)
   - Increase to connection_ramp[2] / request_rate_cps[2].
   - Confirm model-serving worker pools are scaling and GPU utilization <= 85%.

5) Step 4 — Full throughput (+30 to +40 minutes)
   - Allow final ramp step and monitor for steady-state metrics.
   - Mark warmup complete in tenant metadata and remove step header guidance to clients.

Containment and rollback

- Automated containment: edge-sidecar evaluates health_gate every 30s. If any metric breaches: reduce to previous stable step and set cooldown for cooldown_sec.
- Manual rollback: SRE can immediately flip tenant to safe-mode (hard throttle to 10 cps and single connection pool) and open an incident with CS and Eng-Serving-Runtime.

- Emergency isolation: If ingress proxy becomes unhealthy across nodes (ingress CPU > 90% for 2 minutes or 5xx rate > 2% for 1 minute), execute tenant isolation script: /ops/isolate-tenant --tenant tenant-acme-inc --mode drop-new-conns. Notify customer.

Observability and dashboards

Essential charts to have on the warmup dashboard (CS + SRE):
- Ingress: 5xx rate (1m/5m), 50/95/99 latency, connection counts, active streams.
- Edge-sidecar: per-tenant connection pools, queue depth, average request processing time.
- Serving runtime: request queue latency, GPU utilization, batching efficiency, KV cache hit ratio.
- Synthetic probes: success rate, median latency, token throughput.

Suggested Grafana queries (examples)

- 5xx rate: sum(rate(requests_total{status=~"5..",tenant=~\"tenant-acme-inc\"}[1m])) / sum(rate(requests_total{tenant=~\"tenant-acme-inc\"}[1m]))
- Ingress connections: sum(ingress_connections{tenant=\"tenant-acme-inc\"})
- Queue latency histogram: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_processing_seconds_bucket{tenant=\"tenant-acme-inc\"}[5m])) by (le))

Verification checklist (post-warmup)

- Latency: 95th percentile request latency below target (customer-specific, default 350 ms).
- Error rate: 5xx rate < 0.2% sustained for 30 minutes.
- Throughput: achieved >= 90% of projected peak RPS without queue growth.
- Resource: GPU utilization stable and not sustained > 88% for > 10 minutes.
- Client: client observed fewer than 1 retry per 1,000 requests.

Communication templates

- Pre-cutover email to tenant: short checklist, warmup window, expected behavior, contact on-call.
- Post-cutover summary: snapshot of key metrics, anomalies, and next steps.

Escalation path (if warmup fails)

1) CS Lead -> SRE on-call (pager) -> Eng-Serving-Runtime -> Eng-Infra networking lead.
2) If there is immediate customer impact (customer-reported errors affecting revenue), open a P1 and follow incident runbook.

Sample run-command for emergency isolation

# isolate tenant and reduce connections
redwood-ops tenant isolate --tenant tenant-acme-inc --conns 10 --reason "warmup breach"

FAQs and edge cases

Q: Customer uses third-party proxies that pre-open connections.
A: Recommend brokered warmup token returned via header; proxy teams must honor X-Redwood-Warmup to avoid pre-filling connection pools. If impossible, schedule longer step_duration_sec and smaller per-step ramp.

Q: Warmup causes autoscaler thrash (scale up and immediate scale down).
A: Increase scale stabilization window in the tenant autoscaler policy and rely on edge warmup to smooth the observed load.

Q: Token-based workloads vs. many short requests.
A: For token-heavy requests, prioritize KV cache priming: run representative synthetic requests that mirror real token lengths during the earlier warmup steps.
